title: Search Every Entry
content:
What problem does this solve?
Indexing one item at a time works for a tiny list, but it becomes repetitive when the same action should happen to every value. A for loop visits each item in a collection.

Start with the behavior
  for item in ["a", "b", "c"]:
      print(item)
Python takes the first value, stores it temporarily in item, runs the indented body, then repeats with the next value until the list is finished.

The loop variable changes for you
Inside the body, use the loop variable when you mean the current item. Printing the whole list instead will repeat the whole list each time.

Vocabulary after the behavior
A for loop iterates over a collection. The name after for is the loop variable: it refers to the current item during one pass through the body.
concepts: A for loop visits each value in a collection
The indented body runs once per item
The loop variable refers to the current item
Previously learned if/else can be placed inside a loop to decide what to do with each item

examples.title: Visit every item
examples.explanation: The body runs three times, once for each string.

examples.title: Use the current value
examples.explanation: The same operation is applied to each current number.

examples.title: Evidence lines
examples.explanation: The f-string is rebuilt for each current clue.

common_mistakes: Printing the entire list inside the loop instead of the current item
Forgetting to indent the loop body
Trying to manually change the loop variable to reach the next item
Writing one separate print for every known item instead of using the loop

exercises.title: Trace three iterations
hints: The loop body runs once for each list item.
item becomes a, then b, then c in that order.
The three output lines are a, b, and c.

exercises.title: Name the current item
exercises.prompt: Repair the loop header so the body prints red and then blue.
hints: The name in the for header must match the name used inside the body.
The body prints color, so the loop should store each current item in color.
Change the header to for color in items:

tests.message: Use a for loop over items.

exercises.title: Double every number
exercises.prompt:
Loop over the supplied numbers list and print each number multiplied by 2. The output should be exactly:
4
8
12
exercises.starter_code:
numbers = [2, 4, 6]

# Loop over numbers and print each doubled value
hints: Use one loop so the same expression runs for every list item.
Inside the body, multiply the current loop variable by 2.
Use for number in numbers: followed by print(number * 2).

exercises.title: Body runs each time
hints: Both indented print calls are inside the loop body.
For x = 1, Python prints start and 1; then it repeats the whole body for x = 2.
The four lines are start, 1, start, 2.

exercises.title: Print the current item
exercises.prompt: The program prints the entire list twice. Repair only the print line so it prints rope and then torch.
hints: The loop already gives you one current value at a time.
Inside the body, items means the whole list; item means the current string.
Change print(items) to print(item).

exercises.title: Evidence report
exercises.prompt:
Use one for loop and one f-string in the loop body to print exactly:
Evidence: broken lantern
Evidence: drag marks
Evidence: gray dust
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks", "gray dust"]

# Print one formatted Evidence line per clue
hints: Loop over evidence so clue refers to one current string at a time.
Build the line from the current clue, not from a fixed index.
Use for clue in evidence: then print(f"Evidence: {clue}").

tests.expected:
Evidence: broken lantern
Evidence: drag marks
Evidence: gray dust

exercises.title: Evidence Scanner
exercises.prompt:
Build a scanner for the supplied evidence list.

For each clue:
- if the current clue is "gray dust", print FLAG: gray dust
- otherwise print logged: <clue>

Requirements:
- use one for loop over evidence
- make the if/else decision inside the loop
- format each line from the current clue with an f-string
- do not hardcode one output line per list position

After it passes, manually try the same loop with a different three-item evidence list to confirm the behavior transfers.
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "gray dust", "torn cloak"]

# Scan every clue
hints: The loop decides what to do with one current clue at a time, so the comparison belongs inside the loop body.
Compare clue with "gray dust". Both branches should build their text from clue with an f-string.
Use for clue in evidence:, then an indented if clue == "gray dust": / else: with one formatted print in each branch.

tests.expected:
logged: broken lantern
FLAG: gray dust
logged: torn cloak

exercises.success_message: The scanner now combines iteration and decision-making: each item is visited, judged, and reported.
